pages.title: Cold War: origin of term and defining feature
pages.summary: Lists three exam questions on the features and inevitability of the Cold War, whether it has ended, and the causes of its end including the collapse of the USSR. Says Bernard Baruch coined the term, Walter Lippman's book popularised it, Churchill's Iron Curtain speech confirmed it and the 1961 Berlin Wall symbolised it, with nuclear deterrence as its defining feature.

pages.title: Cold War phases, inevitability and responsibility
pages.summary: Describes the Cold War as having warm and cool phases and hurting the Third World, with phases 1949-69, 1969-79 (Detente) and 1979-89, ending with the fall of the Berlin Wall and the Malta summit. Contrasts determinist and social constructivist views on inevitability, and traditionalist, revisionist and post-revisionist views on responsibility.

pages.title: Cold War origins: Bolshevik Revolution, Lenin, Stalin
pages.summary: Says the Cold War was primarily geopolitical, with ideology used heavily, and traces its origin to the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution. Covers Lenin's Communist International, Stalin's socialism in one country, Cominform, Salami tactics, the Molotov-Ribbentrop pact with Hitler and the neutrality pact with Japan.

pages.title: Second World War strains; Baruch and Gromyko plans
pages.summary: Explains how Operation Barbarossa forced the USSR into the war and lists wartime irritants: the delayed second front, Manhattan project secrecy, differences over Europe and the use of nuclear weapons on Japan. The Baruch Plan and Gromyko Plan failed, the USSR tested its first nuclear weapon in 1949 and the nuclear arms race began.

pages.title: First phase events: Berlin, Korea and Vietnam
pages.summary: Describes the Berlin Blockade, NATO, the Warsaw Pact and the Berlin Wall in Europe, and in Asia the 1949 communist victory in China, the Korean crisis and the Vietnam war, which began the decline of US hegemony. Begins Nina Tannenwald's argument on why the USA did not use nuclear weapons.

pages.title: Nuclear taboo, Suez, Cuba and Kennan's containment
pages.summary: Tannenwald holds that a nuclear taboo shows values, norms and public opinion matter, and the Vietnam war led to the breakdown of Bretton Woods and the emergence of the G7. Covers Israel's creation, the Suez crisis as the end of Pax Britannica, the Organisation of American States and the Cuban missile crisis after which Detente started, then begins George Kennan's containment.

pages.title: Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, COMECON, Domino Theory
pages.summary: Kennan's Mr. X telegram urged vigilant and patient containment of Russia. Covers the Truman Doctrine (March 1947), the Marshall Plan (June 1947), COMECON which never worked, and the Domino Theory that justified US involvement in Vietnam.

pages.title: Military pacts and Detente phase treaties
pages.summary: Lists SEATO or Manila Pact (1954) and CENTO or Baghdad Pact (1955) with their members. Defines Detente as relaxation of tension rather than qualitative change, including US-China rapprochement, Ostpolitik, the PTBT, NPT, ABM Treaty, SALT I and the Helsinki Accords.

pages.title: End of Detente; signs of Cold War's end
pages.summary: The 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan ended Detente and the USA announced Star Wars (SDI). Lists signs of the end: the Gulf war with no Soviet opposition, the Berlin Wall's dismantling, the Malta summit, the 1991 Belavezha Accord dissolving the USSR into the CIS, and the CFE and START treaties.

pages.title: Arms treaties, two interpretations, why communism collapsed
pages.summary: Mentions the Nunn-Lugar pact and two interpretations of the Cold War's end: that it ended at Malta, or that the USA won and Russia lost. Says communism collapsed beginning with Solidarity in Poland, gives five reasons, and lists Gorbachev, Reagan and multiple factors as candidates for responsibility.

pages.title: Gorbachev's role: Sinatra Doctrine, Perestroika, Glasnost
pages.summary: Presents Gorbachev as a reformer who wanted to reform, not end, the USSR, honoured by Time magazine and the Nobel Peace Prize. Contrasts the Brezhnev Doctrine of control over Eastern Europe with the Sinatra Doctrine of relaxed control, and defines perestroika and glasnost.

pages.title: Tocqueville, other collapse factors, Reagan's policy
pages.summary: Cites Tocqueville that tyrannies are most endangered when they try to reform, notes the Baltic states left first, and lists oil price depression, an earthquake and Chernobyl as accelerators. Describes Reagan's 'evil empire' rhetoric, a policy to beggar the enemy, the costly Afghan war and Star Wars.

flashcards.front: Who coined the term Cold War, what popularised it, and what was its defining feature?
flashcards.back: Bernard Baruch coined it for USA-USSR relations after the Second World War, and Walter Lippman's book Cold War popularised it. Nuclear deterrence was the defining feature, since nuclear weapons stopped a war-like situation from becoming a direct hot war.

flashcards.front: Was the Cold War inevitable, and who was responsible: how do the competing perspectives answer?
flashcards.back: Determinists say it was inevitable because of fundamental conflict between the superpowers' national interests, while social constructivists call it a tale of misunderstandings, miscalculations and missed opportunities. On responsibility, traditionalists blame the USSR, revisionists the USA and post-revisionists both.

flashcards.front: What were the Baruch Plan (1946) and the Gromyko Plan, and what was the outcome?
flashcards.back: The US Baruch Plan proposed that all countries surrender nuclear materials to a commission under US control, with the USA giving up its weapons once assured. Russia's Gromyko Plan demanded that the USA surrender first; disarmament failed, the arms race began and the USSR tested its first nuclear weapon in 1949.

flashcards.front: Why was the Berlin Blockade of 1949 significant?
flashcards.back: It was the first and last direct confrontation between the superpowers in Europe and a definite US victory. The USA then established NATO in 1949, and the USSR set up the Warsaw Pact in 1955 after West Germany joined NATO, dividing Europe into two military blocks.

flashcards.front: How did Kennan's containment translate into the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan?
flashcards.back: Kennan's 'long telegram' as Mr. X urged vigilant and patient containment of a hostile Russia. The Truman Doctrine (March 1947) sought 400 million dollars to save Turkey and Greece from communism, and the Marshall Plan (June 1947) was the European Recovery Plan, assuming poverty would attract support for communism.

flashcards.front: What was the significance of the Helsinki Accords of 1975?
flashcards.back: The USA and Russia agreed not to try to change the territorial status quo in Europe. The West recognised Russia's legitimate sphere of influence in Eastern Europe, and Russia recognised human rights.

flashcards.front: What was the Sinatra Doctrine and how did it differ from the Brezhnev Doctrine?
flashcards.back: The Brezhnev Doctrine aimed to keep strong control over East European regimes but became unsustainable. The Sinatra Doctrine, named after the song 'My Way', relaxed that control, and once control was removed communism started collapsing.

flashcards.front: Which policies of Reagan towards the USSR are said to have contributed to its collapse?
flashcards.back: Reagan called the USSR an 'evil empire' and followed a policy to beggar the enemy that targeted the core weakness of its crisis-ridden economy. The USA kept the USSR engaged in a costly war in Afghanistan and started Star Wars (SDI).

answers.question: Define the features of the Cold War. Do you think it was inevitable, or the story of misunderstandings and miscalculations?
answers.intro: Bernard Baruch's term described post-1945 USA-USSR relations: a war-like situation that never became direct hot war because of nuclear weapons. Whether this rivalry was inevitable or the product of misunderstandings divides determinist and social constructivist scholars.
body: Features: nuclear deterrence was the defining feature, preventing a third world war, though Nina Tannenwald argues a taboo against nuclear use also mattered. The Cold War was not entirely cold, having warm and cool phases, and the Third World was among its worst sufferers.

Determinists call it inevitable because the superpowers' national interests conflicted fundamentally. Evidence includes the Bolshevik Revolution, Lenin's Communist International, the delayed second front, Manhattan project secrecy and rival visions for Europe and Germany.

Social constructivists call it a tale of missed opportunities. Stalin's socialism in one country signalled no plan for expansion, yet the West distrusted him, and the Baruch and Gromyko plans failed over who should disarm first. After the Cuban missile crisis cooling was necessary and Detente began.

On responsibility, traditionalists blame the USSR, revisionists the USA and post-revisionists both. The notes judge the war primarily geopolitical, with ideology used heavily, as the Berlin Blockade, NATO and the Warsaw Pact split Europe into two military blocks.
answers.conclusion: Structural conflict of interests made rivalry likely, but wartime mistrust and missed chances shaped its form. The post-revisionist view of shared responsibility fits this mixed picture, and it warns that mistrust between nuclear powers needs deliberate management.

answers.question: Discuss the causes of the end of the Cold War in general and the collapse of the USSR in particular.
answers.topic: End of Cold War and Soviet collapse
answers.intro: The Malta summit declaration formally announced the end of the Cold War, though some argue the USA won and Russia lost. Communism collapsed first in Eastern Europe and the USSR then disintegrated in 1991, raising the question of responsibility.
body: Eastern Europe: collapse began with Poland, where Solidarity came to power, and spread country by country. Communism was not the people's choice, was enforced, ran totalitarian regimes, suffered a demonstration effect from better living in western Europe, and caused shortages of even basic commodities.

Gorbachev factor: he wanted to reform, not end, the USSR. He replaced the Brezhnev Doctrine with the Sinatra Doctrine, relaxing control over Eastern Europe, and introduced perestroika (economic restructuring) and glasnost (openness). Tocqueville's view that tyrannies are most endangered when they reform fits this, and the Baltic states left first.

Other accelerators were falling oil prices, a massive earthquake and the Chernobyl disaster. The government's handling of these tragedies bred resentment, and press freedom brought global criticism that challenged its legitimacy.

Reagan's policy: he called the USSR an evil empire and followed a policy to beggar the enemy, targeting its core economic weakness through the costly Afghan war and Star Wars. The 1991 Belavezha Accord then dissolved the USSR into the CIS.
answers.conclusion: Events of this scale cannot be attributed to a single cause. Gorbachev's reforms, Reagan's pressure, economic failure and rejection of imposed communism interacted, so the 'ended at Malta' and 'USA won' readings each capture only part of the truth.
